analysis.one_liner: Stops employer health plans from making Medicare pay first for dialysis patients' care.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the Senate Finance Committee without a hearing or a vote after being introduced late in the 118th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: Some employer health plans pay kidney-dialysis patients a limited amount for dialysis and then steer them to Medicare, which pays less. This bill would change Medicare law so employer plans cannot single out dialysis patients that way: they would have to cover dialysis the same way they cover other care, and remain the primary payer. It would not force plans to include any particular dialysis clinic in their networks.
analysis.who_benefits: Dialysis patients with employer health coverage. Roughly 30,000 such patients each year lose employer coverage or see their employer plan stop paying because plans shift them onto Medicare, which reimburses less than private insurance. The bill would let them keep their full employer coverage and their access to Medicare's coordination-of-benefits protections.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits group health plans from differentiating in benefits against people with end stage renal disease or who need dialysis, based on the diagnosis, the need for dialysis, or any other manner. [S2]
Stops plans from shifting primary responsibility for covering dialysis patients' care onto Medicare, keeping employer plans as the primary payer. [S2]
States the bill's purpose as preserving the breadth of Medicare Secondary Payer Act protections for dialysis patients. [S2]

analysis.who_pays: Employers and the group health plans they sponsor would bear the cost of keeping dialysis patients as primary-paying members instead of shifting them to Medicare, since commercial reimbursement for dialysis is higher than Medicare's.

drawbacks.text: Employers and health plans would pay more: the bill requires them to remain the primary payer for dialysis patients rather than shifting those costs to Medicare, which pays dialysis clinics far less than commercial rates. [S2]

The bill does not change a plan's current ability to limit which dialysis providers it includes in its network, so plans could still steer patients to lower-cost clinics — a carve-out that limits how much protection it provides. [S2]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For dialysis patients, the protection is real: without it, plans can pay a small dialysis benefit and then drop them toward Medicare, reducing their reimbursement rates and their coverage options. The costs fall on employers and insurers, spread across premiums rather than on the patients themselves. The network carve-out means plans retain significant control over where patients can get dialysis, so the bill stops the most aggressive cost-shifting without fully requiring equal access to every provider.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced in September 2024, it was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never acted on it before the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Bill Cassidy introduced the bill on September 11, 2024, with Sens. Booker and Heinrich joining as original cosponsors. [S1]
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day. [S4]
No further action was taken — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025. [S4]
The bill had three additional cosponsors, two Democrats and one Republican. [S3]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and employers who fund group health plans are better off because the bill died: they avoid the cost of remaining the primary payer for dialysis patients, and the existing ability to shift dialysis patients to lower Medicare reimbursement stays in place. Dialysis patients with employer coverage gained nothing.

against.name: Group health plans and insurers
against.role: Employer health plans that shift dialysis patients to Medicare as the secondary payer
against.what_they_did: The bill targets the practice of limiting dialysis benefits and shifting primary coverage to Medicare; insurers have a financial interest in the status quo. [S2]

sides.party_line_note: The lead sponsor was a Republican (Cassidy) and the original cosponsors were two Democrats (Booker, Heinrich), with additional cosponsors split 2 Democratic and 1 Republican — small but bipartisan support, with no recorded opposition on the record.

industries.note: Dialysis companies are reimbursed far more by commercial insurers than by Medicare, so keeping employer plans as primary payers benefits their revenue. The bill preserves their access to commercially insured patients.

industries.industry: Employers and group health plans / health insurers
industries.note: Plans would have to cover dialysis patients without singling them out and remain the primary payer instead of shifting patients to Medicare's lower reimbursement. That saves plans money today and would cost them under this bill, so their interest runs against the patients the bill protects.
When employer plans push dialysis patients onto Medicare, Medicare becomes the primary payer for care it was never meant to cover first; the bill would keep that cost with the employer plans.
